The Basics of Photosynthesis

Diversity of Photoautotrophs

Text description of this image

Plants: Mainly on land; A photo shows forest plants.; Photosynthetic protists: Aquatic; A photo shows photosynthetic protists (aquatic) in the form of kelp, a large, multicellular alga.; Photosynthetic bacteria: Aquatic; A light micrograph at a magnification of 375 shows photosynthetic bacteria (aquatic) of cyanobacteria, which appear as long chains containing green disks.

Chloroplasts: Sites of Photosynthesis

  • Chloroplasts
  • Their green color is from chlorophyll, a pigment (light-absorbing molecule) in the chloroplasts that plays a central role in converting solar energy to chemical energy.
  • Stomata are tiny pores in leaves where carbon dioxide enters, and oxygen exits.
  • Membranes within the chloroplast form the framework where many of the reactions of photosynthesis occur.
  • light-absorbing organelles,
  • the site of photosynthesis
  • found mostly in the interior cells of leaves

Overview of Photosynthesis

Text description of this image

An equation shows that using light energy, photosynthesis converts the reactants 6 C O 2 (carbon dioxide) plus 6 H2O (water) to the products C6H12O6 (glucose) plus 6 O2 (oxygen gas).

A Road Map for Photosynthesis

Text description of this image

The figure shows that oxygen is released during the light reactions in the thylakoids, while carbon dioxide is fixed into sugar during the Calvin cycle in the stroma. In the light reactions, light energy is absorbed in the thylakoids. ATP and NADPH (an electron carrier) are produced and sent to the Calvin cycle, and H2O is split, releasing O2. During the Calvin cycle, which takes place in the stroma, C O 2 is fixed into sugar, using ATP and electrons carried by NAPDH from the light reactions. NADP positive and ADP plus P are then recycled to the light reactions.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum

  • Sunlight, like other forms of radiation, travels through space as rhythmic waves. The distance between the crests of two adjacent waves is called a wavelength.
  • The full range of radiation is called the electromagnetic spectrum.
Text description of this image

10-5 to 10-3 nanometers: Gamma rays; 10-3 to 1 nanometers: X-rays; 1 to 380 nanometers: UV; 380 to 750 nanometers: Visible light; 750 to 106 nanometers: Infrared; 106 to nanometers to 1 meter: Microwaves; 1 to more than 103 meters: Radio waves

The figure also shows a color gradient for visible light, with a pull-out drawing of a wave, shown with regularly spaced and sized peaks and troughs. A wavelength is the distance between two peaks. For the example given, the wavelength is 580 nanometers (orange light). Visible light with its wavelength range and type is listed below:

380: Violet; 400: Violet, shifts to blue as the gradient nears 500 nanometers; 500: Blue, shifting to green, then yellow, and then orange as the gradient nears 600 nanometers; 600: Orange; 700: Red; 750: Red

Chloroplast Pigments

  • The selective absorption of light by leaves explains why they appear green to us.
  • Light of that color is poorly absorbed by chloroplasts and is thus reflected or transmitted toward the observer.
  • Energy cannot be destroyed, so the absorbed energy must be converted to other forms.
Text description of this image

A photo shows light entering a chloroplast, where it is separated into the range of colors in visible light. Red-orange and blue-violet light are absorbed in the thylakoids; green light is either reflected or transmitted, making leaves appear green.

Chloroplasts Pigments

  • Chloroplasts contain several different pigments that absorb light of different wavelengths.
    1. Chlorophyll a participates directly in light reactions and absorbs mainly blue-violet and red light.
    2. Chlorophyll b does not participate directly in the light reactions, but it conveys absorbed energy to chlorophyll a.
  • Chloroplasts also contain a family of yellow-orange pigments called carotenoids, which absorb mainly blue-green light.

How Photosystems Harvest Light

  • Light behaves as waves and discrete packets of energy called photons.
  • When a pigment molecule absorbs a photon, one of the pigment’s electrons gains energy and is now said to be “excited.”
    • An excited electron usually loses its excess energy and falls back to its ground state.
    • Most pigments release heat energy as their light-excited electrons fall back to their ground state.
  • Some pigments emit light as well as heat after absorbing photons.
    • The excited electrons quickly fall back down to their ground state, releasing energy in the form of fluorescent light.
  • Chlorophyll molecules are organized with other molecules into photosystems.
  • Each photosystem has a cluster of a few hundred pigment molecules, including chlorophylls a and b and some carotenoids.
  • This cluster of pigment molecules functions as a light-gathering antenna.
Text description of this image

Figure a shows a photon of light striking a chlorophyll molecule. Absorption of the photon excites the electron, raising it from its starting ground state to an excited state. The electron then falls to its ground state, releasing heat and light (fluorescence).

The Light Reactions of Photosynthesis

Text description of this image

1. A photon of light strikes the reaction center chlorophyll in the first photosystem, exciting two electrons which are trapped by the primary electron acceptor. H2O is split, transferring two electrons to replace the lost electrons in the photosystem and releasing ½ O2 plus 2 H positive. 2. Energized electrons that were trapped by the primary electron acceptor then pass down an electron transport chain to the second photosystem, releasing energy that is used to make ATP. 3. A second photon of light excites two electrons in the reaction center chlorophyll of the second photosystem. These energized electrons are again trapped by a primary electron acceptor, which transfers them to NADP positive, forming NADPH.

How the Thylakoid Membrane Converts Light Energy to the Chemical Energy of NADHP and ATP

Text description of this image

The figure shows that a photon of light strikes the chlorophyll molecules in the first photosystem, embedded in the thylakoid membrane. As the electrons excited by the photon pass to the electron transport chain, H2O is split inside the thylakoid. Two electrons from the splitting of water are transferred to the photosystem to replace the lost electrons, and half O2 is released. As the energized electrons flow through the electron transport chain to the second photosystem, H positive ions are pumped from the stroma across the thylakoid membrane into the thylakoid. These H positive ions fall down their concentration gradient through an ATP synthase in the thylakoid membrane, causing P to be added to ADP, forming ATP in the stroma. The electrons reach the second photosystem at the end of the electron transport chain, where a second photon of light strikes the chlorophyll molecules, again exciting electrons that reduce NADP positive to NADPH (carrying two electrons). NADPH and the ATP formed by the ATP synthase will both be used during the Calvin cycle.

The Calvin Cycle

Text description of this image

The figure lists the following steps:

An enzyme adds each C O2 (from the air) to a five-carbon sugar called RuBP (which has a phosphate group attached to each end). The resulting molecule breaks into two three-carbon molecules (each with one attached phosphate group).; Using energy from ATP and NADPH produced by the light reactions, enzymes convert each three-carbon molecule to the three-carbon sugar G3P (which has one attached phosphate group). As ATP and NADPH are used in this step, ATP goes to ADP plus P and NADPH transfers the two electrons it carries into the step, leaving NADP positive.; For every three molecules of C O2 that enter the cycle, the net output is one G3P sugar. The G3P sugar outputted by the cycle can be converted to glucose and other organic compounds. The other G3P sugars continue in the cycle.; Using energy from ATP, enzymes rearrange the remaining G3P sugars to regenerate RuBP, which is available to begin the cycle again.

Summary

  • Photosynthesis transforms solar energy into chemical energy
  • There is a large diversity of photoautotrophs – all containing chloroplasts
  • Photosynthesis is a coupling of light and dark reactions (Calvin Cycle)
  • Pigments in the chloroplast absorb energy, electrons become “exited” and as they release the energy it is picked-up by NADP+
  • Hydrogens from the light reaction can be used to produce ATP through the electron transport chain.
  • CO2, H2O, and NADPH is used in the Calvin Cycle to produce simple sugars
